Indian Standard
SPECIFICATION FOR JUTE BATCHING OIL

(Second Revision )
0. FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard ( Second Revision ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 15 May 1986, after the draft finalized by the Lubricants and Related Products Sectional Committee had been approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council. 0.2 Jute industry occupies a prominent place in the internal and export It is, therefore, essential that the quality of ,jute goods markets of India. should be such as not to give rise to complaints from these markets. 0.3 Finished jute goods usually contain 2 to 7 percent is an essential material for the batching of jute. by mass of oil, which

0.4 Gunny bags are used for storing of foodstuffs and, therefore, there is a chance of the kerosenic or other objectionable odour from the jute batchFreedom from objectionable ing oil being transmitted to their contents odour is a characteristic which is considered very important by jute mills and users of jute goods. 0.5 This standard was originally issued in 1960. During subsequent years, it was noted that the various countries to which jute products were being exported had felt the need for upgrading the standard by way of prescribing absence from carcinogenic constituents, part;cularly when the jute bags are to be used for packaging of foodstuffs. Limits for pyrene contrnt, ultraviolet absorbance which would indicate polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbon freedom from objectionable odour and limits for distillation range were some of the additional requirements statutorily laid down in some countries for this purpose. Keeping this in view this standard was revised in 1975 incorporating these additional requirements, and classifying the material requirements of the user into two types to take care of the varied countries. 3

`[`II? trst procedurc~ for emulsibility was based on the` work done in the I~l(li;ul Jt~tc 1ndILstric.s' Rrsearch Associatic;n. While revising the standard I)oth the Indian ,Jutc Industries' Rcscarch Association and the suppliers lead Ili,en consulted. Considerable assistance was also taken from the rpquirrments stipldatcd by the Food and Drug Administration of the US 1)cpartmcnt of IIralth, Education and Welfare, Washington D. C.

0.7 The second revision of the standard has been taken up on a request from Indian Jute Industries' Research Association who were facing some difficulties with the current supplies ofjute batching oil. It has been found l)y them that the samples ofjute batchin? oil with density below 0.850 were unsuitable for use due to presence of higher amounts of low boiling fractions. In view of this the density limit has been revised from 0.825 to 0.850. Further it has also been decided to revise the pour point limit and specify differrnt limits for summer and winter months. In addition to this the initial boiling point for Type 1 has been specified in this revision. 0.8 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS : Z-1%0*. The number of significant places rrtained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

APPENDIX [ Tuble 1, [tern (vi) ]
EMULSIFICATION A-O. OUTLINE A-0.1 The OF THE METHOD

A

TEST

method consists in emulsifying jute batching oil with aqueous sodium oleate solution at room temperature at a specified ratio of oil and sodium oleate, and visually examining the stability of the 10 percent dilute emulsion after being left undisturbed at room temperature for 24 hours.

A-l. A-l.1

APPARATUS

Emulsification Vessel - A tapered vessel, open on top, made of brass or enamelled metal and of dimensions shown in Fig. 1. It has an approximate capacity of 1 500 millilitres.
A-l.2 Stirrer - Made of brass and of dimensions shown in Fig. 1. The three adjustable blades ( A, B and C in Fig. 1 ) are set 25 mm apart in the vertical direction at an angle of 60" to one another by means of screws. When fitted to the vessel for emulsification tests, there shall be a clearance of not more than 3 mm between the tip of the top blade and the side of the vessel when the bottom blade is almost flush with the base of the vessel. The stirrer shall be located in this position during the emulsification test. A-l.3 Electric Motor-A motor may be provided with a rheostat to control speed of stirring. There shall be a suitable arrangement to couple the stirrer to the spindle of the motor without excessive wobbling. A-2. REAGENTS

A-2.1 Sodium Oleate Solution - Prepare a 4 percent ( m/v ) solution of sodium hydroxide ( see IS : 376-1976* ) in distilled water (see IS : 107019771_ ) and to this solution add the equivalent quantity of pure oleic acid ( equivalent mass 282 ) drop by drop with stirring. Dilute and mix the resulting gel-like substance with the requisite quantity of distilled water to yield a homogeneous solution containing 15 g of sodium oleate per 100 ml of solution. Prepare a stock solution and use it for a number of emulsification tests. *Specification for sodium hydroxide, analytical
tSpeci&ation for watrr for general laboratory reagent ( second revision ). IN' ( secod revision ).

A-3. A-3.1 PROCEDURE Carry out the test at the prevailing room temperature,

A-3.2 Connect the motor to the stirrer and adjust the latter inside the tapered vessel so that the three blades are 25 mm apart with the bottom blade almost f-lush with the bottom of the vessel. Place 10 ml of sodium oleate solution in the vessel and set the stirrer in motion at about 400 rev/ min by adjusting the rheostat. Take 300 ml of the oil in a separating funnel and add to the sodium oleate solution drop by drop until a gel is formed. Increase the rate of addition thereafter and add the entire quantity of the oil in the course of an hour. Add about 2 ml of distilled water every 5 minutes to ensure the presence of an optimum quantity of water in the gel. Keep an account of the volume of water thus added. Periodically, note the stirring efficiency and adjust the rheostat to give efficient stirring. The speed of stirring shall not be less than 150 rev/min when the gel has reached the maximum consistency. A-3.3 Continue mixing the gel and add 290 ml ( including the of distilled water to the gel Maintain the stirring between The resulting emulsion is nearly for 5 minutes after the addition of the oil volume added during the gel formation ) taking about 15 minutes for this addition. 150 and 400 rev/min during this period. 50 percent in oil content.

A-3.4 Falter the 50 percent emulsion through a thin pad of cotton wool placed inside a 150-mm bowl diameter glass filter funnel ( see IS : 1541lc378* ) and wait until the whole of' the emulsion is filtered. Stir the filtered emulsion with a glass rod or by rotating the container by hand, Transfer quickly 100 ml of this emulsion iuto a 500-ml graduated cylinder provided with a stopper, and dilute with 400 ml of distilled water. Place the stopper in p.osition and mix the contents uniformly by inverting the stoppered cylinder about ten times. Allow the resulting 10 percent emulsion to stand on the laboratory bench undisturbed for 24 hours and examine it at the end of this period. A-3.5 The oil shall be regarded as having passed the emulsification no free oil has separated on top as examined visually. test if

A-3.5.1 The stability of emulsion shall be determined visually. For the purpose of this test, the emulsion shall be regarded as stable if there is no separation of free oil from the emulsion. Creaming of the emulsion, that is, separation into a thick emulsion layer on top and a thin white coloured aqueous layer at the bottom shall not be confused with separation of free oil, A creamed emulsion becomes homogeneous on shaking or agitation whereas free oil, if present, separates from the emulsion after a short period.

IS : 1758 - 1986 A-3.5.2 In the above emulsification test, the ratio of oil to 15 percent on the basis of sodium oleate soap solution is 30 : 1, and when calculated 30 percent strength, this ratio becomes 60 : 1. Soap of the latter strength is used in the commercial preparation of emulsions in the jute industry and the jute industry require jute batching oils which give satisfactory emulsion with a minimum of 60 parts by volume of oil to every one part by volume of a 30 percent soap solution.

B-2.3 Potassium Iodide Solution - Prepare a fresh solution by dissolving 10 g of potassium iodide free from potassium iodate, in 100 ml of water. B-2.4 Starch Solution - Make a paste of 0.5 g of soluble starch in cold water, pour in 100 ml of boiling water, boil for 5 minutes, cool and bottle. The solution should be prepared afresh every two or three days. B-2.5 Standard Sodium Thiosnlphate Solution0.1 N. Weigh accurately about 25 g of sodium thiosulphate crystals ( Na&.Os,5HsO ) and dissolve in water which has been boiled to free it from carbon dioxide and make to 1 000 ml. Store the solution in a cool place in a dark-coloured stock bottle with a guard tube filled with soda lime. After storing the solution for about one week, filter and standardize it as prescribed in B-2.5.1.

IS : 1758 - 1986 B-2.5.1 Weigh accurately about 0.2 g of finely ground potassium dichromate which has been previously dried to constant mass at 105 * 2"C, in a clean and dry conical flask, and dissolve in a small quantity of water. Add FO ml of water, 4 ml of concentrated hydrochloric acid and 20 ml of potassium iodide solution. Titrate the mixture with sodium thiosulphate sob tion, using starch solution as an indicator towards the end. The end-point is taken when the blue colour changes to green. B-2.7 Acetic Acid - Glacial, 99 percent, having a melting point of 14.8% and free from reducing impurities. Determine the melting point of the acetic acid and test it for reducing impurities as follows:

a)

Melting Point Determination - Take a 15 cm long test tube and fill it to about two-thirds with the acetic acid. Insert into the acid a thermometer satisfying the requirements specified in B-l.1 through a cork stopper fitting the test tube. The amount of acid should be at least double the quantity required to cover the bulb of the thermometer when the bottom of the latter is 12 mm from the bottom of the test tube. Suspend this tube within a larger test tube through a cork, Cool the acid by immersing the assembly in ice water until the temperature is lO'C, then withdraw the assembly from the ice water and stir the acid rather vigorously for a few moments, thus causing the supercooled liquid to crystallize partially and give a mixture of liquid and solid acid. Take thermometer readings every 15 seconds and consider as the true melting point that temperature at which the reading remains constant for at least 2 minutes. Test for Reducing Impurities ( Potassium Permanganate Test ) - Dilute 2 ml of the acetic acid with 10 ml of water and add O-1 ml of 0.1 N potassium permangante solution and maintain at 27 * 2�C. The test shall be taken as having been satisfied if the pink colour is not discharged at the end of 2 hours. Gas Dry. 11

IS : 1758 - 1986 B-2.9 Iodine Trichloride ( ICla )

B-2.10 Wijs Iodine Monochloride Solution - Prepare this solution by one of the following two methods, and store in a glass-stoppered bottle in a cc~ol place, protected from light:
a ) l)issolve

13 g of iodine in one litre of acetic acid, using gentle heat, if necessary, and determine the strength by titration with standard sodium thiosulphate solution. Set aside 50 to IOU ml of the solution and introduce chlorine gas into the remainder until the characteristic colour change ( a sudden disappearance of colour ) occttrs and the halogen content is nearly doubled as asc`ertained again by titration. If the halogen content has been more than doubled, reduce it by adding the requisite quantity ot' the iodine-acetic acid solution. A slight excess of iodine does not harm but avoid an excess of chlorine.

Example - If the titration of 20 ml of original iodine-acetic acid solution requires 22 ml of standard sodium thiosulphate solution, 20 ml of the finished Wijs solution should require between 43 and 44 ml ( and not more than 44 mI) of the same sodium thiosulpate solution.

b)

As an alternative method for preparing Wijs solution, dissolve 8 g of iodine trichloride in approximately 450 ml of acetic acid. Dissolve separately 9 g of iodine in 450 ml ofacetic acid, warming; if necessary, and then cool. Add gradually the iodine solution to t11e iodine trichloride solution until the colour has changed to reddish-brown. Add 50 ml more of lodine solution and dilute the mixture with acetic acid till 10 ml of the mixture is equivalent to 20 ml of standard thiosulphate solution when the halogen content is estimated by titration in the presence of an excess of potassium iodide and water. Heat the solution to 100% for 2il minutes and cool. Prevent access of water vapour in preparing the solution. or Chloroform with it. Inert to Wijs solution

Add 25 ml of Wijs solution and replace the glass stopper after wetting with potassium iodide solution; swirl for intimate, mixing and allow to stand in the dark at room temperature for 2 h with occasional swirling. C

[ Tuble1, item (ix) ]
ULTRAVIOLET [ Adapted from C-O. GENERAL FDA ( UV ) ABSORBANCE Regulation .No. 121.2589 TEST of USA ]

INSTRUCTIONS

C-O.1 Because of the sensitivity of the test, the possibility of errors arising from contamination is great. It is of the greatest importance that all glassware be scrupulously cleaned to remove all organic matter, such as oil, grease detergent residues, etc. Examine all glassware, including stoppers and stopcocks under ultraviolet light to detect any residual fluorescent contamination. As a precautionary measure it is recommended practice to rinse all glassware with purified iso-octane immediately before use. No grease is to be used on stopcocks or joints. Great care to avoid contamination of',jute batching oil samples in handling and to assure absence of any extraneous material arising from inadequate packaging is essential. Because 13

C-1.1 GIassware - Assorted beakers, separatory funnels fitted with tetrafluoroethylene polymer stopcocks, graduated cylinders and volumetric flasks of ZOO-ml capacity. C-1.2 Reservoir - A 500 taper male fitting at bottom ing to the nitrogen supply. columns described in C-l.3 both be equipped with glass C-l.3 Chromatograpbic ml capacity reservoir having a 24/40 standard and a suitable ball joint at the top for connectThe female fitting of the chromatographic and the male fitting of the reservoir should hooks.

Columns

C-1.3.1 A chromatographic column made from nominal 1.3 cm outside diameter x 75 cm glass tubing tapered at one end and joined to a 2-mm bore tetrafluoroethylene polymer stopcock. The opposite end is flanged and joined to a female 24/40 standard taper fitting. This provides for accommodating the 500 ml reservior described above. C-1.3.2 A chromatographic column made from nominal 1.7 cm outside diameter x 115 cm glass tubing tapered at one end and joined to a 2-mm bore tetrafluoroethylene polymer stopcock. The opposite end is Ranged and joined to a 2-5 cm outside diameter x 9.0 cm glass tube having a female 24/40 standard taper fitting. This provides for accommodating the 500 ml reservoir described above. C-l.4 Spectrophotometer - A spectrophotometer equipped to automatically record absorbance of liquid samples in 1 cm path lengthcells in the spectral region of 280-400 nm with a spectral slit width of 2 nm or less. At an absorbance level of about 0.4, absorbance measurements shall be repeatable within 5 0.01 and accurate within f O-05. Wavelength measurements shall bc repeatable within * 0.2 nm and accurate within & 1.0 nm. Instrument operating conditions are selected to realize this performance under dynamic ( automatic ) recording operations. Accuracy of absorbance measurements is determined at 290, 345 and 400 nm, using potassium chromate as the reference standard. C-1.5 Spectrophotometer Cells length of I*00 f 0,005 cm or better. Place about 1 kg of silica gel in a large column and wash with contaminant-free benzene until a 200 ml sample of the benzene coming off the column will pass the ultraviolet absorption test for benzene. This test is performed as stipulated under C-2.1. When the silica gel has been sufficiently cleaned activate the gel before use by placing the 1 kg batch in a shallow container in a layer not greater than 2.5 cm in depth and heating in an oven ( Caution : Explosion Hazard ) at 130% for 16 h and store in a vacuum desiccator. Reheating about once a week is necessary if the silica gel is repeatedly removed from the desiccator. C-2.1.10 Aluminium Oxide ( 180-75 the following procedure: micron )f Purified and activated by

Place about 1 kg of aluminium oxide in a large column and wash M'ith contaminant-free benzene until a 200 ml sample of the benzene coming off the coIumn will pass the ultravioIet al)corption test for benzene. This test is performed as stipulated under C-2.1. ( Caution : Remove benzene from adsorbent under vacuum to minimize explosion hazard in subsequent heating. When the aluminium oxide has been suflicicntly cleaned and freed of solvent, and activate it before use by placing the 1 kg batch in a shallow container in a layer not greater than 2.5 cm in depth. Heat in an oven at 130�C for 16 hours. Upon removal from heat store at atmospheric pressure over 80 percent ( by mass ) sulphuric acid in a desiccator for at least 36 hours before use. This gives aluminium oxide with between 6 and 9.5 percent votatiles. This is determined by heating a weighed sample of the prepared aluminium oxide at 1 lOO"C for 2 hours and then quickly reweighing.
